final.title: Pairing problems: marriage and checkerboard
paragraphs: A pairing problem is decided by what each pair must contain, not by how many pieces there are in total. A checkerboard has 64 squares, and 32 dominoes, each covering two neighboring squares, cover it completely. Cut off two opposite corners and 62 squares remain. Thirty-one dominoes cover 62 squares, so the numbers seem to fit and people start laying dominoes down, but no number of failed attempts would ever prove a covering impossible.

The colors decide it. Neighboring squares are always different colors, so every domino, wherever it lands, covers exactly one dark square and one light square. Opposite corners are the same color, so removing them takes away two squares of one color. What remains is 32 squares of one color and 30 of the other, and 31 dominoes would need 31 squares of each color. That balance is simply not there, so the board cannot be covered, and counting the colors settles the question before any domino is placed.

The Russian marriage problem has the same structure in a form where it is easy to see. A village has 32 bachelors and 32 unmarried women, and the matchmaker has arranged 32 marriages. Then two bachelors die, and the question is whether she can arrange 31 marriages among the 62 survivors. Every marriage pairs one man with one woman, and there are now 30 men and 32 women, so at most 30 marriages are possible and two women are left over. Sixty-two people would make 31 pairs only if anyone could pair with anyone, but each pair needs one person from each group, so the smaller group sets the limit.

This is analogical transfer, with the marriage story as the source problem and the checkerboard as the target. The parts map one to one: men and women are the two colors of squares, marriages are dominoes, and the two dead bachelors are the two missing corners. Each leftover square corresponds to a woman without a partner. Because the mapping is complete, the reasoning from the source carries straight over, and rearranging the dominoes more cleverly cannot help, since the imbalance between the two kinds rules out the last pair.

A shoe store that sells shoes only as matched pairs shows the same logic. Someone wheels in a cart with 30 left shoes and 32 right shoes and asks how many pairs can be sold. The answer is not 31 just because there are 62 shoes in all. A pair needs one of each kind, so the lefts and the rights are counted separately and the smaller pile decides: 30 pairs, with two right shoes left on the cart however they are shuffled. The shoes are the squares or the people, and a pair is a domino or a marriage. Whenever the counts of the two kinds are unequal, some pieces are left over, so the whole method is to ask what each pair must contain and count those things.

final.title: Converging solution (radiation, fortress, lightbulb)
paragraphs: Duncker's radiation problem sets two demands against each other. A patient has an inoperable malignant tumor in his stomach, and a kind of ray can destroy the tumor if it arrives all at once at a high enough intensity. At that intensity the healthy tissue the rays pass through on the way is destroyed too. At lower intensities the rays are harmless to the tissue, but they do nothing to the tumor either. The tumor needs high intensity and the tissue needs low intensity, so no single ray can satisfy both, and only 10% of participants reach the answer without help.

The answer is to send several low-intensity rays from different directions so that they converge on the tumor at the same time. Each ray is weak enough to pass through healthy tissue safely, and where they meet, their combined strength destroys the tumor. The strong effect exists only at the point where the weak parts meet.

A chef who wants to brown the sugar on one spot of a dessert faces the same shape. The dish and table underneath are delicate and would scorch under a hot flame. One strong burner would brown the spot and ruin everything it passes over, and one gentle lamp keeps everything safe but browns nothing. Several gentle lamps aimed at the same spot from different sides solve it, because anywhere along the way only one lamp shines and the surroundings feel something mild, while at the point where all the beams cross the warmth adds up enough to brown the sugar. When something needs a strong effect in one place and a weak effect everywhere else, the strength is split into weak pieces that travel separate paths and arrive together.

The fortress problem has this same structure. A rebel general knows his whole army could take a dictator's fortress, but the roads are mined so that only small groups pass safely, and a large force would blow up the road and the neighboring villages. He divides the army into small groups, sends them along different roads, and has them arrive at the same time. The fortress is the tumor, the small groups are the low-intensity rays, the roads are the paths through tissue, and the mines are the healthy tissue.

Noticing a good analogy is hard. After reading the fortress story, only 30% solved the radiation problem, against 10% without it, and 70% did not see the correspondences by themselves. Gick and Holyoak described three steps: noticing the analogy, which is the most difficult, mapping the parts of the source onto the target, and applying the mapping to produce a parallel solution. Failing at any one blocks the answer. When participants were told to think about the story they had read, success rose to 75%, so noticing is the main barrier.

Similarity of surface features makes noticing much easier. In the lightbulb problem, a strong laser aimed at a broken filament would break the fragile glass around it, while a weak laser would not fuse the filament. Rays and lasers, tumors and filaments, and tissue and glass are close enough that the link comes to mind easily. Eighty-one percent of participants who knew the radiation problem solved the lightbulb problem, against 10% of the control group, which had no source. The radiation problem worked far better as a source than the fortress story, which helped only 30%, because it shares both the structure and the surface features of the target.

final.title: Base rates and Jack
paragraphs: A base rate is how common each category is in the population. When you judge what category someone belongs to, the starting point should be those numbers, and a description should adjust them, not replace them. This is hard because a description is vivid and a base rate is a dry number, so the description tends to push the number out of the judgment completely.

In a group of 100 people with 70 lawyers and 30 engineers, one person picked at random has a 30% chance of being an engineer, and people get this right. People use base rate information if it is all that is available, but when a description is available they disregard the base rate.

Jack is a 45-year-old man, married with four children, generally conservative, careful and ambitious, and uninterested in political and social issues. He spends most of his free time on hobbies, including home carpentry, sailing and mathematical puzzles. People say Jack is an engineer, because his careful nature and love of puzzles fit the engineer stereotype, and that fit outweighs the base rate. But nothing in the description rules out a lawyer. A lawyer could be careful and conservative and enjoy puzzles, and the group still contains many more lawyers than engineers. The 70 and 30 are still true after reading about Jack, so the description has to be weighed against them and cannot settle the question by itself.

A party of 100 people, 90 in the chess club and 10 on the basketball team, makes the point clear. One person picked at random is tall, quick on their feet and loves jumping, and almost everyone guesses basketball because the description sounds like a basketball player. But 90 chess club members fill the room, and with that many people, plenty of them are tall, quick and love jumping too. Before any description, the chance of basketball was 10 out of 100. The description pushes the guess up from that low starting point, perhaps by a lot, but it has to be very convincing to end up above even. A good fit makes basketball more likely than it was a minute ago, not more likely than chess club. The crowd's numbers say where to begin and the description says how far to move.

This is the representativeness heuristic, judging class membership by resemblance. Robert wears glasses, speaks quietly and reads a lot, and people say librarian and ignore that America has about 2.2 million farms and 120,000 libraries. Farmers far outnumber male librarians, so even if Robert's traits are somewhat more common among librarians, a randomly picked man is much more likely to be a farmer. The mistake in every case is letting the vivid description replace the dull numbers entirely.

final.title: Conjunction rule (Linda)
paragraphs: The conjunction rule says that the probability of two events occurring together cannot be higher than the probability of either single event alone. A conjunction means two things being true at once. The rule is easy to state and easy to break, because a more detailed story feels more likely even though it is less likely. Each added detail narrows the possibilities, and narrower things are less probable.

Linda is 31 years old, single, outspoken and very bright, and she majored in philosophy. As a student she was deeply concerned with issues of discrimination and social justice, and she also took part in antinuclear demonstrations. People are asked which is more probable: that Linda is a bank teller, or that Linda is a bank teller who is active in the feminist movement. Because Linda sounds like a feminist, the second option feels more like her, and 82% pick it, which breaks the rule.

The groups show why. Everyone who is a bank teller makes up one large group, and some of those people are active in the feminist movement while many are not. The feminist bank tellers are a smaller group sitting inside the larger group of all bank tellers. Anyone in the smaller group also belongs to the larger one, so the larger group can never have fewer members, and a group contained inside another can never be more probable than the one containing it. Bank teller alone must be at least as probable as feminist bank teller.

Nested regions on a map work the same way. A friend who is in a coffee shop in Chicago is in Illinois, so the statement that she is in a Chicago coffee shop is true only when the statement that she is in Illinois is true. Illinois is a large area, Chicago sits inside it, and the coffee shop sits inside Chicago. Each added detail draws a smaller region that holds fewer of the places she might be, and she could be in Illinois in a hundred ways that have nothing to do with Chicago. A detailed story can feel more believable because it paints a clearer picture, but it can only be equally likely or less likely than the broader version it lives inside.

The error is the representativeness heuristic. Linda resembles a feminist, so the resembling option is judged more likely and people stop thinking about the sizes of the categories. How well a story fits a person says nothing about whether a combination can be more probable than one of its parts.

final.title: Sample size (hospital question)
paragraphs: Sample size controls how far a percentage can drift from the true rate by chance. A town has two hospitals. In the larger one about 45 babies are born each day, and in the smaller one about 15. About 50% of all babies are boys, but the exact percentage varies from day to day. For one year, each hospital recorded the days on which more than 60% of the babies born were boys, and the question is which hospital recorded more such days: the larger, the smaller, or about the same.

Most people get this wrong. Fifty-six percent said about the same, and the larger and the smaller hospital were each chosen by 22%. The reasoning is that both hospitals have the same true rate of about 50% boys, so both should have unusual days equally often. That fixes on the 50% that applies to both and overlooks that the question is about day-to-day variation, which depends on how many babies are born each day as well as on the average rate.

With about 15 births in a day, chance can easily tilt a day heavily toward boys, so a day with more than 60% boys happens fairly often. With about 45 births, chance variations even out over more births, and the share of boys stays nearer 50%. The smaller hospital therefore records many more days over 60% boys, and the correct answer is the smaller hospital.

A basketball player who makes about half her shots over a season shows the same thing. In a game with only six shots, one or two lucky bounces put her well above half, and that happens in plenty of games. In a game with sixty shots, lucky and unlucky shots keep canceling each other out, and finishing above 60% would take unusual luck for a long stretch, which is rare. Her ability is the same in both games. What differs is how many chances there are for luck to even out. The six-shot game is the small hospital, the sixty-shot game is the large one, and the days above 60% are the unusually lucky games.

The law of large numbers states that the larger the number of individuals randomly drawn from a population, the more representative the resulting group will be of the entire population. A small random sample can be thrown off by a few unusual cases, so it may differ a lot from the population. The true rate describes the long run and does not promise that every short stretch will look like it. People who answered about the same expected every sample to look like the population, which is the representativeness heuristic applied where sample size matters.

final.title: Probability as a ratio (jellybeans)
paragraphs: Your chance of winning is the number of winning items divided by the total number of items, not the number of winning items. The error comes from the fact that a count is easy to see and a proportion takes a little work, so people judge by what looks like more.

In the jellybean study, participants could earn up to $7 by receiving $1 every time they drew a red jellybean, and each time they chose between two bowls. One bowl held 1 red jellybean out of 10, so the odds were 1 in 10. The other held 7 red jellybeans out of 100, so the odds were 7 in 100, or 0.7 in 10. One in 10 is 10% and 7 in 100 is 7%, so the first bowl gives the better chance of a red bean. Yet most participants chose the 7 in 100 bowl. It has more red beans, seven instead of one, so it seems to offer more chances, even though it also holds many more white beans that hide those reds.

Their choice was influenced by considerations other than probabilities. People paid attention to the number of winning beans instead of their proportion, and by choosing by appearance they lowered their real chance of winning.

Two raffles at a school fair show the same trap. In the first drum there are 20 tickets and 3 win, and in the second there are 100 tickets and 12 win. Twelve winning tickets sounds far better than three, but a ticket is one single pull from the drum, and what matters is how crowded the drum is with losers. Three winners out of 20 is 15 out of every 100, which is 15%, and 12 winners out of 100 is 12%. The small drum with fewer winners is the better bet, because its winners make up a bigger share of what you might pull out.

A count of winners means something only once you know how big the whole pile is. Writing each option as winners out of total, converting to a percentage, and comparing the percentages avoids the error, and the red counts alone should never be compared.

final.title: Expected utility
paragraphs: Decision making means making judgments that involve choices between different courses of action. Utility is the measure of how good an outcome is for the person who chooses it, referring to outcomes that are desirable because they are in the person's best interest. An option with higher utility leads to a better outcome for that person. Expected utility theory begins from the claim that people are rational. It holds that if people have all the relevant information, they will make the decision that results in the maximum expected utility, where expected utility combines how good each outcome is with how likely it is. In its early form, utility meant maximum monetary payoff, so the best choice was the one that paid the most money on average.

The procedure is to multiply the value of every possible outcome of an option by its probability, add the products, and pick the option with the largest total. The advantage is that the approach offers specific procedures for determining the best choice and tells what a fully rational decision maker would pick. That makes it a benchmark against which real choices can be compared.

Deciding each morning whether to carry an umbrella, with a 30% chance of rain, works this way. Carrying it costs a small, certain annoyance. Leaving it at home costs nothing if the sky stays dry, but a soaking and a ruined afternoon if it rains. The question is not only whether it will rain but how much each result would matter and how likely it is. If getting soaked bothers you a great deal, even a 30% chance of it can outweigh the small nuisance, so you carry the umbrella. If you will be indoors all day, the soaking matters little and you leave it. No money is involved. The values are how good or bad each outcome is to you, and the chances act as weights on those values.

The comparison with real behavior shows the limits of the theory. Utility is not necessarily money, because people find value in other things, such as safety, fairness or how they feel about a choice. People are not utility maximization machines. They gamble in casinos all the time even though they know the odds are very much against them, because they value the thrill or the chance at a big win. How a choice is worded can also pull them away from the larger total.

The refugee convoy dilemma makes the point sharply. Sending the convoy to the second camp would save 1,000 people but cost 100 in the first camp, so rerouting has utility 1000 minus 100, which is 900, and not rerouting has utility 100 minus 1000, which is minus 900. Expected utility theory says to reroute. Ritov and Baron (1999) found that 63% did not choose to send the convoy to the second camp, because actively causing harm weighs more than failing to prevent a larger one. The theory is a strong standard but a weak description of how people really choose.

final.title: Inductive evidence strength
paragraphs: Inductive reasoning is reasoning based on observations, going from particular cases to a general conclusion. Scientists do this deliberately, making observations, collecting data and proposing a general rule that fits the many cases they have seen. Ordinary people do it constantly too, predicting what will happen from what has happened in the past, and some of it happens automatically, without deliberate thought. The conclusion is only probably true, never definitely true, so the real question is always how strong the support is.

Three things decide the strength of an inductive argument. The first is the representativeness of the observations, meaning how well they stand for the whole category. Many observations from a narrow group can still lead to a wrong conclusion, so a big pile of evidence from one corner of a category does not help much. The second is the number of observations, since more observations give stronger support. The third is the quality of the observations, since careful and accurate observations count for more, and sometimes one very compelling, high-quality observation can carry a lot of weight.

Reviews of a new pizza place show all three. The conclusion being built is that all their pizzas are great, a general claim drawn from the few pizzas other people happened to try. If every review comes from people who ordered the same cheese pizza on Friday nights, a hundred of them still say little about the rest of the menu, because they do not stand for the whole category. Twenty reviews support the conclusion better than two. One detailed review from someone who tried many dishes and described them carefully can count for more than a pile of one-line ratings.

Quality can outweigh quantity because an inductive conclusion is a general claim built from particular cases. One clear counterexample, such as one soggy, burnt pizza from that kitchen, can prove it false however many happy reviews came before. That is why inductive conclusions are always open to revision, and why a new observation can overturn a conclusion drawn from earlier ones. Judging an inductive argument means checking how representative the observations are, how many there are, and how good each one is.
